3. METHODOLOGIES, ANALYSES AND LICENSING BASIS EVENTS

This chapter of the safety evaluation (SE) summarizes the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission
(NRC or Commission) staffs review and evaluation of the Long Mott Generating Station (LMGS)
preliminary safety analysis report (PSAR) chapter 3, “Methodologies, Analyses, and Licensing
Basis Events.”

3.1. Methodologies and Analyses
3.1.1. Probabilistic Risk Assessment

Section 3.1.1 of the LMGS PSAR summarizes the scope, methodology, and technical adequacy
of the probabilistic risk assessment (PRA). The PSAR section discusses how the advanced
non-light-water reactor (non-LWR) PRA standard was applied to LMGS and includes a
summary of the results from the PRA self-assessment. The PRA is used as the primary tool for
implementing the risk-informed and performance-based licensing modernization project (LMP)
methodology described in Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) 18-04, “Risk-Informed Performance-
Based Technology Inclusive Guidance for Non-Light Water Reactor Licensing Basis
Development,” Revision 1 (ML19241A472), as endorsed with clarifications in Regulatory Guide
(RG) 1.233, “Guidance for a Technology-Inclusive, Risk-Informed, and Performance-Based
Methodology to Inform the Licensing Basis and Content of Applications for Licenses,
Certifications, and Approvals for Non-Light-Water Reactors,” Revision 0. RG 1.233 includes
guidance for identifying licensing basis events (LBEs), determining the classification of
structures, systems, and components (SSCs) and their special treatments, and evaluating
defense-in-depth (DID) adequacy.

The LMGS PRA provides an integrated assessment of overall plant risk against the following
risk evaluation criteria described in NEI 18-04, section 3.2.2, step 7b, and addressed in PSAR
section 4.1:

e The total mean frequency of events exceeding a site boundary dose of 100 millirem
(mrem) (0.1 roentgen equivalent man (rem)) from all LBEs should not exceed one/plant-
year;

e The average individual risk of an early fatality within one mile of the exclusion area
boundary (EAB) from all LBEs should not exceed 5x10°/plant-year; and

e The average individual risk of latent cancer fatalities within ten miles of the EAB from all
LBEs should not exceed 2x10°/plant-year.

The applicable regulatory requirements at the construction permit (CP) application stage related

to the use of PRA to inform the licensing basis of a non-LWR design and the risk to public
health and safety from plant operation are as follows:

The relevant guidance documents related to the use of PRA for this CP application includes:

e RG 1.233, “Guidance for a Technology-Inclusive, Risk-Informed, and Performance-Based
Methodology to Inform the Licensing Basis and Content of Applications for Licenses,
Certifications, and Approvals for Non-Light-Water Reactors,” Revision 0 (ML20091L698),
which endorses with clarifications, the guidance in NEI 18-04, “Risk-Informed
Performance-Based Technology Inclusive Guidance for Non-Light Water Reactor
Licensing Basis Development,” Rev. 1 (ML19241A472).

e RG 1.247, “Acceptability of Probabilistic Risk Assessment Results for Non-Light-Water
Reactor Risk-Informed Activities,” For Trial Use (ML21235A008); and

e RG 1.253, “Guidance for a Technology-Inclusive Content-of-Application Methodology to
Inform the Licensing Basis and Content of Applications for Licenses, Certifications, and
Approvals for Non-Light-Water Reactors,” Revision 0 (ML23269A222), which endorses
with clarifications and additions NEI 21-07, “Technology Inclusive Guidance for Non-Light
Water Reactor Safety Analysis Report: For Applicants Utilizing NEI 18-04 Methodology,”
Rev. 1 (ML22060A190).

NEI 18-04 describes an expanded role for PRA for non-LWRs beyond current Commission
policy for potential applications under 10 CFR Part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and
Utilization Facilities.” Following NEI 18-04, the applicant uses the PRA to develop or confirm the
ESs, safety functions, key SSCs, and adequacy of DID. Because the PRA plays an important
role in the plant design process, the NRC staff audited how LME developed and used the PRA
to develop the preliminary LMGS licensing basis following the LMP approach, and applied
specific risk insights to the LMGS design. The NRC staff followed the guidance in appendix A of
RG 1.253, to audit the LMGS CP stage PRA within the context of the LMP framework. Appendix
A provides guidance on the expected scope, level of detail, and quality of a PRA suitable for the
CP stage, recognizing that the plant design is still evolving and that the PRA model is inherently
limited in maturity. The NRC staff applied RG 1.247, which endorses, with clarifications, the
American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) and American Nuclear Society (ANS) RA-S-
1.4-2021 non-LWR PRA standard, to evaluate the technical adequacy and completeness of
each PRA element performed. The NRC staff's review of the PSAR therefore focused on
assessing whether the PRA provides a technically sound foundation to support LMP-related
activities, specifically, the identification and evaluation of LBEs, classification of SSCs according
to safety significance, and the establishment of adequate DID. At the CP stage, the NRC staff
determines whether the preliminary PRA follows RG 1.233 and appendix A of RG 1.253,
thereby providing a provisional basis for assessing risk acceptance criteria (e.g., quantitative
health objectives (QHOs), frequency-based thresholds for LBEs), and to inform early-stage
design and licensing decisions through systematic risk insights, given that uncertainties related
to parameter, model, and completeness have not yet been fully characterized or assessed. The
NRC staff's audit focused on whether the PRA in use at the CP stage, provides a reasonable
technical basis for ongoing design development and establishes a foundation for future updates
and expanded scope at the operating license (OL) application stage.

3-2

 The PRA insights and results described in PSAR section 3.1 includes inputs to multiple PSAR
chapters where risk information is used as an input to the LMGS design and safety analysis. In
PSAR section 4.1, LME incorporates PRA results into the overall assessment of plant-level risk
and in PSAR section 4.2, LME describes its assessment of the adequacy of DID. PSAR

section 5.1 describes LME’s application of PRA insights to the classification of SSCs. Similarly,
in section 5.2 of the PSAR, LME identifies the safety-significant PRA safety functions (PSFs),
including safety-related (SR), non-safety-related SSCs with special treatment (NSRST), and
non-safety-related with no special treatment (NST) functions derived from PRA results. In PSAR
sections 6.2 and 7.1, LME describes the use of PRA data to establish reliability and capability
targets. In PSAR sections 6.4 and 7.3, LME applies PRA-derived safety functions to define
functional requirements and design criteria, and PSAR section 11.4 describes the use of PRA
insights to support analyses related to plume exposure pathway emergency planning Zone size.
As such, the PRA described in PSAR section 3.1 is instrumental in supporting development of
the LMGS LMP licensing basis, ensuring that the design, classification, and operational
evaluations are systematically informed by quantitative risk insights and aligned with the overall
risk-informed licensing approach.

3.1.1.1 Technical Evaluation

Section 3.1 of the PSAR summarizes the LMGS CP stage PRA and introduces how the PRA
results and insights are linked to safety analysis and design evaluation throughout the PSAR.
Specifically, this section presents the PRA overview, key modeling assumptions, and a
summary of PRA results essential to the licensing basis under the LMP framework. The
information in PSAR section 3.1, supports the risk-informed identification of LBEs and provides
the quantitative basis for determining safety-significant functions, establishing DID, and defining
reliability and capability targets for important SSCs. The NRC staff considered the applicable
regulations and guidance identified above to determine whether the LMGS PRA was developed
using generally accepted methods and reflects an appropriate level of technical rigor to support
its intended use at the CP stage. Specifically, the NRC staff evaluated PSAR section 3.1 against
RG 1.233, RG 1.253 sections A.3 and A.5, and RG 1.247. These guidance documents outline
the acceptable practices for PRA development and application within the framework of the LMP
and provide expectations for the PRA scope and level of detail in support of a CP application. In
particular, RG 1.253 sections A.3 and A.5, indicates that the PRA description submitted with a
CP application, be a high-level overview or summary that addresses PRA quality, scope,
intended applications, and overall acceptability. The applicant is expected to demonstrate that
the PRA was developed in a manner commensurate with the maturity of the design, and that the
PSAR includes sufficient information to support the CP-level safety determinations.

The NRC staff assessed the acceptability of the LMGS PRA by evaluating the PRA scope, level
of detail, PRA elements, and plant representation and configuration control in an integrated
manner. The NRC staff's review of the PRA scope includes the risk metrics used, the
radiological source terms considered, the internal event causes (hazard groups) analyzed'; and
the plant operating states (POSs) evaluated.

1 As described in appendix A of RG 1.253, an applicant for a CP may disposition certain hazards by crediting design
basis hazard levels (DBHLs) in lieu of explicitly modeling these hazards in the PRA or accounting for them through a
risk-informed supplementary evaluation.

The NRC staff's review of the level of detail includes the extent of modeling necessary to
capture plant behavior, system interactions, and interdependencies with sufficient resolution to
support intended applications.

The NRC staff's review of the PRA elements includes the technical analyses that support the
development and quantification of the PRA model, consistent with its intended use at the CP
stage.

The NRC staff's review of the plant representation and configuration control includes the degree
to which the PRA accurately reflects the current design and the mechanisms in place to manage
configuration changes as the design evolves.

Consistent with RG 1.253, the PSAR describes the intended use of the LMGS PRA during the
design and construction phases:

e Chapter 3 provides a high-level overview of the PRA model and presents the set of
LBEs, which are derived from and informed by PRA event sequence (ES) families.

e Chapter 4 presents the integrated risk results and compares them to the three
cumulative plant performance criteria outlined in NEI 18-04.

e Chapter 5 identifies the preliminary set of PSFs, including those fulfilled by both SR and
NSRST SSCs. The chapter also documents risk-significant SSCs credited for meeting
frequency-consequence (F-C) targets and cumulative risk criteria.

e Chapters 6 and 7 discuss the reliability and capability targets for SR and NSRST SSCs
and describe how PRA results and insights informed the development of these targets
and their associated special treatments.

The NRC staff's evaluations and conclusions regarding the PRA-related content presented in
other sections of the PSAR are documented in the corresponding sections of the NRC staff's
SE. This section focuses specifically on the scope, level of detail, and quality of the PRA
information provided in chapter 3 of the PSAR.

To support the NRC staff's review, the NRC staff conducted an audit focused on the PRA and
its supporting documentation. The audit provided the NRC staff with access to PRA materials
and facilitated direct discussions with the applicant to clarify technical issues related to the PRA.
The NRC staff's audit included the LMGS PRA model that the applicant developed using the
Computer Aided Fault Tree Analysis System (CAFTA) software. The NRC staff focused its audit
of the PRA model on the model structure, development methodology, and quantification. The
NRC staff also audited (ML##) selected sensitivity analyses to assess the design’s robustness
at the CP stage and to better understand the uncertainties inherent in the PRA modeling.

As discussed below, based on the NRC staff's review of the PSAR, as confirmed in the audit,
the NRC staff determined that the LMGS PRA was developed in a manner consistent with
applicable guidance and in reasonable conformance with the non-LWR PRA standard
ASME/ANS RA-S-1.4-2021, as endorsed by RG 1.247. The LMGS PRA demonstrates that the
risk associated with the LMGS site and preliminary Xe-100 design is acceptably low and

provides meaningful risk insights in support of implementing the LMP methodology described in
NEI 18-04.

Additionally, the NRC staff determined that LME followed the guidance provided in RG 1.253,
and addressed the eleven minimally acceptable PRA elements outlined in table A-1 at a level
sufficient for the CP stage. The NRC staff's evaluation of each element is described below. LME
performed a self-assessment to ensure the LMGS PRA conformed to these eleven elements in
accordance with the non-LWR PRA standard ASME/ANS RA-S-1.4-2021. LME described in
PSAR section 3.1.1.1, that its self-assessment was performed following the guidance in

NEI 20-09, “Performance of PRA Peer Reviews Using the ASME/ANS Advanced Non-LWR
PRA Standard,” Revision 1 (ML20302A115), which is endorsed in RG 1.247. A summary of the
NRC staff's review of LME’s self-assessment is provided below.

Unlike the surrogate risk metrics commonly used in LWR PRAs, such as core damage
frequency and large release frequency, the LMGS CP application employs risk metrics focused
on offsite radiological consequences from ESs involving the release of radioactive material.
These consequence-based metrics are aligned with those used in LWR level 3 PRAs but
exclude consideration of radiological or other impacts on on-site personnel. At this stage of the
design development, the applicant evaluated the following radionuclide source terms in the
LMGS PRA:

e Fuel pebbles in the reactor
e Circulating activity within the helium pressure boundary (HPB)
e Radionuclides plated out on surfaces within the HPB

ASME/ANS RA-S-1.4-2021, as endorsed by RG 1.247, with exceptions, provides guidance for
PRA radionuclide source terms for non-LWRs. The NRC staff reviewed the PSAR and audited
supplemental materials to confirm and understand the information in the PSAR. Based on the
NRC staff's review, the NRC staff determined these source terms to be reasonable and
sufficient for the CP stage PRA because they were developed with approved methods and are
consistent with the ASME/ANS RA-S-1.4-2021, as endorsed, with exceptions, by RG 1.247.A
summary of the NRC staff's review of LME’s mechanistic source term analysis is provided
below in PRA element 9 and the NRC staffs review of the mechanistic source term
methodology is in section 3.1.4 of this SE.

PRA Element 1 — Initiating Event Analysis

As described in RG 1.247, the objective of the initiating event (IE) analysis is to identify and
characterize events that could challenge safe plant operation during any POS and require
effective mitigation by plant equipment and personnel to prevent or to mitigate a release of
radioactive material. This includes both events that may occur at the plant and those with a
credible probability of occurrence.

PSAR section 3.1.1.2 summarizes the hazards that were screened out of the PRA, the hazards
that were screened into the PRA, and the hazards addressed through alternative approaches
such as design-basis hazard level (DBHL) framework. Consistent with RG 1.253, section A3.3,
at the CP stage some PRA elements, such as external hazards, were not completed. PSAR

section 3.1.1.2 describes the internal IEs that the applicant considered for all sources of
radionuclides and POSs that are identified in PSAR sections 3.1.1.2 and 3.10, and section 3.11,
respectively. The LMGS IE analysis focused on internal events during full power operation that
could impact the fuel in the reactor, circulating activity within the HPB, and radionuclides plated
out on surfaces within the HPB.

To further understand the description in PSAR section 3.1.1.2 and PSAR table 3.2-2, the NRC
staff audited Document ID number 000897, “Probabilistic Risk Assessment: Initiating Event
Analysis — Preliminary Scoping,” Revision 4. The audit focused on confirming the characteristics
and attributes of the IE analysis to ensure the analysis aligns with the non-LWR PRA standard
ASME/ANS RA-S-1.4-2021 and RG 1.247 and is consistent with information in the PSAR. The
NRC staff examined the approach and method applied in the IE analysis, ensuring they are
reasonable and consistent with accepted industry practices; the NRC staff also confirmed during
the audit that the assumptions are reasonable, and the analysis aligns with the preliminary plant
design to the extent possible.

Specifically, during the audit the NRC staff focused on the systematic approach used to develop
a comprehensive list of potential internal IEs during full power operation, including those
affecting the reactor core, such as the steam generator (SG) tube leaks and main steam line
breaks. The NRC staff examined how LME used multiple data sources, such as
NUREG/CR-6928 (MLO70650650), and relevant non-LWR and U.S. Department of Energy’s
standard modular high temperature gas reactor PRAs, to ensure LME’s review was
comprehensive, and to understand how system-level design reviews were applied to identify
plant-specific initiators.

During the audit, the NRC staff also reviewed the methods used to group similar IEs and
estimate their frequencies using generic data supplemented with design-specific information.
The NRC staff focused on the assumptions, data sources, and treatment of parametric and
modeling uncertainties in the IE analysis. The NRC staff's audit identified that the IE
identification, grouping, and frequency estimation processes were conducted in a structured and
traceable manner consistent with the non-LWR PRA standard. The NRC staff confirmed in the
audit, that the analysis includes a reasonable set of potential initiators, appropriately reflects
current design information, and identifies key sources of uncertainty for follow-up and
refinement at the OL application stage.

Based on the NRC staff's review, the NRC staff determined the IE analysis to be reasonable
because the information in PSAR section 3.1.1.2, is consistent with RG 1.253 and the analysis
was performed in accordance with RG 1.247, as appropriate for a preliminary design and
applicable to the CP stage, as follows:

e The IE analysis includes detailed identification and characterization of IEs suitable for
the design stage.

e LME logically grouped IEs based on similarity in mitigation requirements.
e LME used reasonable estimates for IE frequencies.

e LME identified and qualitatively characterized sources of model uncertainty related to the
IE analysis.

As LMGS advances from preliminary design towards operation, the IE analysis and its
underlying assumptions are expected to be updated and refined using increasingly detailed
plant information.

PRA Element 2 - Event Sequence Analysis

As described in RG 1.247, the objective of the ES analysis is to model, in chronological order to
the extent practical, the different possible potential progressions of events following the IE.
These ESs lead either to successful prevention or to the release of radioactive material. The
analysis will account for the availability of plant systems and operator actions based on defined
success criteria (SC) and established plant operating procedures, including emergency and
abnormal operating procedures.

The LMGS ES analysis, which at the CP stage is limited to full-power conditions, is described in
PSAR sections 3.1.1.2 and 3.1.1.3, and PSAR table 3.2-2. PSAR section 3.1.1.3 describes that
LME performed ES modeling and quantification using the Electric Power Research Institute
(EPRI) Phoenix Architect, which includes CAFTA, UNCERT, FRANX, and FTREX. The ES
analysis integrates POSs, IEs, safety functions, and the success or failure of SSCs, culminating
in end states that may involve potential release of radioactive material. The primary output of
the ES analysis is a set of event trees (ETs), which delineate possible event progressions. Each
ET represents a time-independent, system-level response to a specific IE. The results provide
essential inputs for plant risk quantification. PSAR table 3.2-2 provides the initiator and a brief
word description of the LBE sequences.

To further understand the description in the PSAR, the NRC staff audited Document ID
number 002414, “Probabilistic Risk Assessment: Event Sequence Analysis — Preliminary
Scoping,” Revision 4. The audit focused on the characteristics and attributes of the ES analysis
to ensure that the analysis aligns with the non-LWR PRA standard ASME/ANS RA-S-1.4-2021
and RG 1.247 and is consistent with information in the PSAR. The NRC staff examined the
approaches and methodologies used in the ES analysis, ensuring that they are reasonable,
technically defensible, and consistent with established industry practices. The NRC staff also
confirmed in the audit, that the assumptions are reasonable and the analysis reflects a level of
detail suitable for the preliminary plant design.

Specifically, during the audit, the NRC staff focused on the modeling of event progressions
following the initiation of an IE for full-power conditions. The NRC staff focused on the
development of ETs representing plant responses to various IEs, the identification of key
radionuclide release barriers, and the integration of safety functions supporting reactivity control,
primary circulator flow, core heat removal, and the HPB. The NRC staff examined how the
applicant defined fuel damage, the associated end states, and the mission times applied to
active and passive heat removal sequences.

The NRC staff further assessed the use of design stage assumptions, treatment of modeling
and completeness uncertainties, and the documentation of SC for key safety functions. The
NRC staff's audit confirmed that the ES analysis was structured and traceable, reflected the

PRA Element 3 - Success Criteria Analysis

As described in RG 1.247, the objective of the SC analysis is to establish the minimum
functional requirements for each key safety function and the systems that fulfill these functions
to prevent or mitigate radioactive release following an IE.

To further understand LME’s SC analysis, the NRC staff audited Document ID number 001994,
“Xe-100 Probabilistic Risk Assessment: Success Criteria Development,” Revision 3. The audit
focused on the characteristics and attributes of the SC analysis to ensure the analysis aligns
with the non-LWR PRA standard ASME/ANS RA-S-1.4-2021 and RG 1.247 and is consistent
with information in the PSAR. The NRC staff assessed the SC analysis approach to confirm that
the SC are based on reasonable engineering analyses and that the assumptions are
appropriate, and the analysis aligns with the preliminary plant design.

Specifically, during the audit, the NRC staff focused on the minimum functional requirements for
SSCs necessary to maintain critical safety functions during full-power conditions. The NRC staff
focused on the methods and assumptions used to establish performance requirements for key
safety functions, reactivity control, primary circulator flow, core heat removal, and the HPB, and
the corresponding SSCs that maintain radionuclide barriers such as the HPB. The NRC staff
assessed how both active and passive systems were treated in the analysis, including the
determination of SC for active systems and the engineering basis for passive system
performance.

The NRC staff also audited the assumptions and uncertainties in the SC analysis to confirm that
they are reasonable for the CP stage, given the preliminary nature of the design. Due to the
preliminary nature of the design, the NRC staff focused on understanding the treatment of
modeling and completeness uncertainties and the traceability of the analytical bases supporting
the SC. Overall, the NRC staff used the audit to confirm that the SC analysis appropriately
reflects the LMGS design’s capability to fulfill essential safety functions and that the approach
aligns with the non-LWR PRA standard for the current stage of design maturity.

Based on the NRC staff's review, the NRC staff determined the SC analysis to be reasonable
because the SC analysis is consistent with RG 1.253, and the analysis was performed in

accordance with RG 1.247, as appropriate for a preliminary design and applicable at the CP
stage, as follows:

e The SC analysis addresses fundamental safety functions, supporting SSCs, and
operator actions.

e LME identifies relevant sources of model uncertainty.

e LME documented the SC analysis to provide traceability of the technical basis at a level
sufficient for the CP stage.

As LMGS advances from preliminary design towards operation, the SC analysis and its
supporting assumptions are expected to be updated based on the final design.

PRA Element 4 - Systems Analysis

As described in RG 1.247, the objective of the systems analysis (SY) is to identify and model
the various combinations of failures that could prevent a system from fulfilling its functions as
defined by the SC. The system model incorporates hardware, instrumentation, and their
associated failure modes, as well as human failure events (HFEs) that could impair system
performance. Basic events representing equipment and HFEs should be developed in sufficient
detail to capture dependencies among systems and to highlight specific equipment or human
actions that significantly impact the system’s ability to perform its intended functions.

3.1.3.1 Technical Evaluation

The NRC staff's evaluation of the GFQ TR approved the use of TR 008585 for the preliminary
safety analysis of DBAs consistent with 10 CFR 50.34 (a)(4) for the Xe-100 design, subject to
one limitation (ML25262A060,). This limitation requires that the review of input parameters for
the Flownex and GOTHIC input models be performed as part of the review of the PSAR.
Accordingly, the evaluation presented here is focused on verifying that the GFQ TR limitation is
addressed adequately in the PSAR for the LMGS reactor design, confirming that the Flownex
and GOTHIC models used in the PSAR analyses remain consistent with those approved in the
GFQ TR, and evaluating any new modeling elements introduced in the PSAR that were not
previously reviewed in the GFQ TR.

The thermodynamic analysis methodology follows the EMDAP in RG 1.203 and includes two
system analysis codes - Flownex and GOTHIC - to evaluate short-term and long-term
responses of the plant under postulated transient conditions. In the short-term phase, the
applicant uses the Flownex thermal-hydraulic code to model transient behavior over periods
ranging from several minutes to multiple hours, during which plant parameters are still evolving
due to control and shutdown rod motion, valve realignments, circulator behavior, and changes in
SSC status. This phase represents conditions when active systems may continue to influence
the plant response. If the short-term analysis demonstrates that forced cooling is maintained at
the end of the transient, the applicant does not perform an additional long-term evaluation.

If, however, the Flownex end state reflects transition to a non-forced-circulation condition, the
long-term passive-cooling phase is evaluated using the GOTHIC code. In this phase, the
applicant models the plant’s behavior for up to 30 days, representing bounding LBE conditions.
The PSAR explains that in the long-term phase, the plant parameters are not significantly
changing, and the core heat is removed passively.

Importantly, the PSAR clarifies that both the Flownex short-term and GOTHIC long-term
analyses begin at time zero. There is no handoff or data transfer from the short-term simulation
